client: I've been avoiding my favorite café because just walking past it makes my heart pound like crazy. It's where my ex and I used to meet all the time, and now I feel this wave of panic whenever I even think about going in. I know it's just a coffee shop, but I can't seem to shake this reaction no matter how much I tell myself to get over it.
therapist: It sounds like this café has become deeply tied to those painful memories, and your body is reacting strongly even though you know logically it’s just a place. Let’s explore together how we can gently challenge those automatic thoughts and help you regain a sense of control over these feelings. You’re not alone in this, and it’s okay to take small steps.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client:
I know you're right that it's just a place, but every time I walk by that café, my chest gets tight and I feel like I can't breathe. It's where my ex and I used to meet all the time, and now just seeing the sign makes me remember all the good times we had before everything fell apart. 

I guess I could try going in there again, but what if I just end up feeling worse? It's been six months and I still can't shake these feelings.
therapist: I hear how deeply this space connects to those memories, and it’s understandable that it feels overwhelming right now. Let’s take it step by step—maybe we can start by imagining walking by the café together and noticing what thoughts and feelings come up, without rushing to go inside. You’re doing brave work by facing this, and it’s okay to move at your own pace.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know if just imagining walking by the café will help. Every time I even think about that street, my chest gets tight and I start remembering everything that happened there. It's not just about the café - the whole neighborhood feels tainted now. Maybe this is too much too soon?
therapist: It sounds like this has become much bigger than just one café—the whole area now carries that weight of painful memories. Let’s slow down and focus on what feels manageable right now, even if it’s just acknowledging how hard this is without pushing yourself further. Your feelings are valid, and we can work at a pace that feels safe for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
It's just... I don't know if avoiding the whole neighborhood is really helping either. Every time I take the long way around to avoid passing by that café, I feel both relieved and guilty at the same time. Like I'm letting the memories control me instead of dealing with them. 

But the thought of going back there makes my chest tighten up so much I can barely breathe. I keep imagining seeing her sitting at our usual table with someone else, even though I know that's probably not going to happen.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to move forward and feeling overwhelmed by the possibility of facing those memories head-on. The tightness in your chest tells me this is still really raw for you, and that’s okay. Let’s explore how we can gently challenge those vivid images and help you feel more grounded when these thoughts arise.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Yeah, that tightness in my chest is always there when I think about what happened. Part of me wants to push through and deal with it, but another part is terrified that if I really let myself feel it, I'll just fall apart completely. I keep seeing flashes of that day in my mind, and it's like my body reacts before I can even stop it. 

The idea of "gently" facing it sounds nice in theory, but I don't know how to do that without getting completely overwhelmed. Every time I try, it feels like I'm drowning. How am I supposed to challenge something that still feels so immediate and painful?
therapist: I hear the conflict in your voice—part of you wants to move forward while another part feels completely unprepared for that flood of emotions. Your mind and body are reacting strongly to those memories, and we can work on grounding techniques to help you feel more in control when those overwhelming moments come up. It's okay that this still feels raw; healing doesn't have to mean pushing through all at once. Let's find small, safe ways to face this piece by piece.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate that you’re taking this slow with me, but I’m still not sure if grounding techniques will really help. When those memories hit, it feels like I’m drowning, and I can’t even think straight enough to try anything. It’s like my body just takes over, and I freeze. I want to believe there’s a way through this, but it feels impossible right now.
therapist: It sounds like those moments feel completely overwhelming, like you’re swept away before you even have a chance to catch your breath. Let’s focus on small steps—maybe starting with just noticing when those feelings begin to rise, without needing to fix them right away. You’re not alone in this, and we’ll find a way to help you feel more anchored, even in the midst of the storm.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the feelings first, but when the anxiety hits, it's like my brain just goes blank. I can't even think straight enough to notice what's happening - it all just crashes over me at once. And honestly, the idea of just observing it without trying to fix it makes me more anxious because then I feel like I'm losing control.
therapist: I hear how frightening that blank, overwhelmed feeling is—like you're completely at the mercy of the anxiety before you can even catch your breath. Let’s try something different: instead of observing in the moment, we can practice grounding techniques when you're feeling calmer, so they become more automatic when those waves hit. You’re describing this with such clarity, which tells me part of you is already beginning to notice these patterns, even if it doesn’t feel that way in the moment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about practicing when I'm calm, but in the moment it feels impossible to remember any techniques. My brain just goes completely blank, like all the tools disappear. And honestly, sometimes I worry that if I practice too much when I'm okay, it'll make me think about anxiety more and actually make things worse.
therapist: I can hear the frustration in your voice—it makes complete sense that when anxiety takes over, all those practiced tools feel out of reach. That worry about focusing "too much" on anxiety is understandable, but remember: gentle preparation isn’t about inviting anxiety in, it’s about helping your nervous system feel safer when those moments arise. Let’s find ways to make these tools feel more natural, like second nature, so they’re there even when your mind goes blank.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying about making the tools feel more natural, but honestly, sometimes when the anxiety hits, it's like my brain just shuts down completely. I've tried deep breathing and grounding techniques before, but in the moment it feels impossible to remember them or believe they'll help. It's frustrating because part of me knows these things should work, but another part is convinced nothing will make the anxiety stop.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting these tools to help and feeling completely disconnected from them when you need them most—that frustration comes through clearly. Let’s shift focus for a moment: instead of techniques, can we explore what might help you feel even slightly more anchored *before* those overwhelming moments build? Sometimes small, simple reminders can create a bridge when the bigger tools feel out of reach.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I like the idea of small reminders, but honestly, I'm not sure what would actually help. When I'm spiraling, everything feels pointless - like even if I had a reminder, I'd just ignore it or think it's stupid. Maybe I'm being too negative, but that's how it feels in the moment. 

The worst part is that I know logically these are just thoughts, but they feel so real and overwhelming when they hit. It's like my brain betrays me.
therapist: I hear how exhausting this battle feels—when those thoughts take over, even the idea of help can seem meaningless, and that hopelessness comes through in your voice. Let’s acknowledge how real and overpowering those moments are while also gently holding space for the part of you that *knows* they’re thoughts, not facts. That awareness, even when it feels distant, is actually a sign of strength we can build on.
